text: Our prover works in a field of 31 bits. The signature we want to verify, Plum, computes in a prime field of 199 bits.
cap: Our prover works in a field of 31 bits. The signature we want to verify, PLUM, computes in a prime field of 199 bits.

text: Take one multiplication in that big field. A prover built on the big field would do it in one step. That is the cost we would like to pay.
Our prover must split each number into 7 limbs of 30 bits. Schoolbook multiplication then forms 7 times 7, or 49, limb products.
One Plum verification at the 80-bit level calls the Griffin hash 1052 times. Griffin is built from exactly these big-field multiplications.
cap: One PLUM verification at the 80-bit level calls the Griffin hash 1052 times. Griffin is built from exactly these big-field multiplications.

text: Run as plain software, the verification takes 7.08 billion guest cycles. On a 24 gigabyte laptop, the prover runs out of memory after about 1 minute 45 seconds.
The standard fix is a precompile. It is a dedicated circuit for one operation, called from the program like a system call. We built one for the Griffin permutation.
With it, the proof finishes in 14.25 minutes, the mean of 3 runs. So far the story is simple. The precompile makes it faster.
Now swap the hash instead. A control arm uses shah three, computed in ordinary software, with no hash precompile at all.
cap: Now swap the hash instead. A control arm uses SHA-3, computed in ordinary software, with no hash precompile at all.

text: The control finishes in 13.05 minutes. The arm with the precompile is slower, in every run we took.
A precompile removes cycles from the program. But its own circuit still has to be proved, and its rows are not counted as cycles.
The prover commits a table of cells, and its work grows with the number of cells. We call that number the trace area.
A precompile changes two terms. It removes core area, the cells the removed cycles would have used. It adds chip area, the cells of its own circuit.
It pays exactly when the core area removed exceeds the chip area added, each weighted by its cost per cell.
Check it against plain software. Each Griffin call removes about 6.6 million cycles. It adds 14 rows of 3819 columns, about 53 thousand cells. The precompile pays by a wide margin.
Now check it against shah three. The Griffin arm runs 13 percent more cycles. It also commits 56 million chip cells that the control never pays.
cap: Now check it against SHA-3. The Griffin arm runs 13 percent more cycles. It also commits 56 million chip cells that the control never pays.

text: Both terms are larger, so the Griffin arm loses for any cost per cell. One inequality gives both outcomes.
Could we simply count cycles instead? A second primitive in Plum shows why not. It is the power-residue symbol.
cap: Could we simply count cycles instead? A second primitive in PLUM shows why not. It is the power-residue symbol.

text: A dedicated chip for it runs in 365 cycles. The software loop takes 6549. By cycles, the chip looks 17.9 times cheaper.
By trace area, the chip commits 382 multiplication columns per symbol. The loop commits 261. The chip adds area instead of removing it.
The two measures point in opposite directions. So the rule must be stated in trace area, not in cycles.
Where can removed core area come from? It comes from emulation, from splitting big numbers into limbs.
With ell limbs, one multiplication costs between ell and ell squared native multiplications. When ell is 1, there is nothing to remove.
cap: With ℓ limbs, one multiplication costs between ℓ and ℓ² native multiplications. When ℓ is 1, there is nothing to remove.

text: So the rule predicts something we can test. A precompile can only pay for a primitive whose field does not match the prover's. A mismatch is necessary, but not sufficient.
We test the necessary direction first, in execute mode. The cost per multiplication should be small at 1 limb and grow with the number of limbs.
At 1 limb, a multiplication costs 19 guest cycles. At 7 limbs, it costs 3121. That is a factor of 164.
Across 4 widths, 2, 4, 7, and 8 limbs, the cost grows as ell to the power 1.30. That lies inside the band.
cap: Across 4 widths, 2, 4, 7, and 8 limbs, the cost grows as ℓ to the power 1.30. That lies inside the band.

text: Next, three precompiles over the same field. The Griffin chip is mismatched, and nothing else serves it. It pays, with 56.4 times fewer cycles in execute mode.
The field-multiplication chip is mismatched too. But the host already ships a 256-bit multiplication precompile, so it does not pay.
The power-residue chip is the open case. A fused chip would pay its control overhead once, instead of 261 times. Whether that wins is an experiment we specify, not one we ran.
One more test is still open. The rule forecasts that a matched-field precompile will not pay in a full proof. We state that forecast before the run.
So the precompile makes Plum verification finite to prove on a laptop. Is that enough for an anonymous credential? Not yet.
cap: So the precompile makes PLUM verification finite to prove on a laptop. Is that enough for an anonymous credential? Not yet.

text: The proof we can afford is a stark proof, and it is not zero-knowledge. The wraps that add zero-knowledge are Groth 16 and Plonk. Both rely on pairings, so neither is post-quantum.
cap: The proof we can afford is a STARK proof, and it is not zero-knowledge. The wraps that add zero-knowledge are Groth16 and PLONK. Both rely on pairings, so neither is post-quantum.

text: The wrap also fails at recursive compression. Our Griffin chip overflows the toolchain's fixed recursion shapes. Regenerating them is a one-time job, not a memory limit.
The zee kay vee em's flexibility does not show up in time either. Recompiling the static circuit takes about 0.3 seconds. What differs is how much must be re-audited after a change.
cap: The zkVM's flexibility does not show up in time either. Recompiling the static circuit takes about 0.3 seconds. What differs is how much must be re-audited after a change.

text: All proving times are at the 80-bit level, which is not a deployment level. Each is the mean of 3 runs on one 24 gigabyte laptop.
The positive results assume the Griffin circuit's constraints are sound. That assumption is open. The negative results do not depend on it.
The practical rule is short. Before building a precompile, compare the core area it removes with the chip area it adds.
Three questions remain open. They are the matched-field proof, the fused power-residue chip, and a post-quantum zero-knowledge wrap. The thesis is called, When does a precompile pay?
